content: Your doctor has prescribed ampicillin, an antibiotic, to treat your infection. This medication can be administered either by injection into a large muscle, such as the buttock or hip, or through an intravenous (IV) infusion. The IV infusion involves adding the drug to a fluid that drips into your vein via a needle or catheter over approximately 30 minutes, and this process is typically repeated four to six times daily. Ampicillin works by eliminating bacteria responsible for various infections, including pneumonia, meningitis, and infections of the urinary tract, gastrointestinal tract, skin, bones, joints, blood, and heart valves. In some cases, this medication may be prescribed for other conditions; consult your doctor or pharmacist for further details. Your healthcare provider will monitor the effectiveness of the treatment and any potential side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how your infection and symptoms respond to the medication. Before starting ampicillin, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to ampicillin, penicillin, cephalosporins, or any other medications. Additionally, provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are currently taking, especially other antibiotics, allopurinol (Lopurin), anticoagulants like warfarin (Coumadin), atenolol (Tenormin), oral contraceptives, probenecid (Benemid), rifampin (Rifadin), sulfasalazine, and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of kidney or liver disease, allergies, asthma, blood disorders, colitis, stomach issues, or hay fever. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. Should you become pregnant while taking ampicillin, contact your doctor immediately. If you have diabetes and regularly test your urine for sugar, use Clinistix or TesTape, as Clinitest tablets may yield false positive results due to the medication. Before administering ampicillin, inspect the solution carefully. It should appear clear and free of any floating particles. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Instead, use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to follow your healthcare provider's instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not discontinue the treatment on your own, as this could worsen your infection and potentially lead to hospitalization. Do not alter your dosing schedule without consulting your healthcare provider. If you encounter a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may advise you to stop the infusion. Ampicillin may cause side effects. Notify your doctor if you experience any of the following minor side effects, especially if they are severe or persistent: upset stomach, diarrhea, vomiting, or a mild skin rash. However, if you experience any of the following severe side effects, contact your healthcare provider immediately: severe skin rash, itching, hives, difficulty breathing or swallowing, wheezing, unusual bleeding or bruising, headache, dizziness, seizures, or a sore mouth or throat. If you are receiving ampicillin intravenously, your healthcare provider will likely supply you with several days' worth of medication at a time. Store the medication in the refrigerator or freezer as instructed. Before using your next dose, remove it from the refrigerator one hour in advance and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to reach room temperature. If you are instructed to store additional doses in the freezer, transfer a 24-hour supply to the refrigerator each day for the following day's use. Do not refreeze the medication. If you are receiving ampicillin intramuscularly, your healthcare provider will provide specific storage instructions. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry place when not in use, and store all medications and supplies out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will also instruct you on the safe disposal of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving ampicillin via an IV or under the skin, it is important to recognize the signs of a catheter-related infection, which occurs at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin. Notify your healthcare provider immediately if you notice any of the following symptoms near the catheter site: tenderness, warmth, irritation, drainage, redness, swelling, or pain. Ampicillin is also marketed under the brand name Principen®.
